Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

his pronoun

classical

Quint. 1.9.5: paedagōgum ejus percussit
Cic. Sen. 31: ex ejus linguā melle dulcior fluēbat ōrātiō

ejus

pronoun: genitive of is; it does not change with the thing owned

his (someone else’s)

Use ejus when “his” is not the subject of the clause: Crates struck paedagōgum ejus, the boy’s tutor. When “his” is the subject’s own, Latin uses suus: “Esau ran to meet frātrī suō (his own brother) … and clasped collum ejus (his, the brother’s, neck)”.

Other words

  • suus, sua, suum — his (own), referring to the subject

    pronoun (possessive, reflexive), first and second declension · classical · Liv. 2.10.11: incolumis ad suōs trānāvit; Cic. Off. 3.59: invītat Canius postrīdiē familiārēs suōs

    Refers back to the subject of its clause, or in reported speech and purpose clauses to the subject of the main verb. It agrees with the thing owned: ad suōs, to his own men.

  • illīus — his (that man’s)

    pronoun: genitive of ille · also used · classical

    For a stronger or contrasting “his”.

Examples

  • Currēns itaque Esau obviam frātrī suō, amplexātus est eum: stringēnsque collum ejus, et ōsculāns flēvit.

    So Esau ran to meet his brother and embraced him, and clasping his neck and kissing him, he wept.Vulg. Gen. 33.4

  • ut Cratēs, cum indoctum puerum vīdisset, paedagōgum ejus percussit

    as Crates, when he saw an ignorant boy, struck the boy’s tutorQuint. 1.9.5

  • ex ejus linguā melle dulcior fluēbat ōrātiō

    from his tongue flowed speech sweeter than honeyCic. Sen. 31

  • ita sīc armātus in Tiberim dēsiluit multīsque superincidentibus tēlīs incolumis ad suōs trānāvit

    So, armed as he was, he leapt into the Tiber, and under a hail of missiles swam across unhurt to his own men.Liv. 2.10.11

  • invītat Canius postrīdiē familiārēs suōs, venit ipse mātūrē, scalmum nūllum videt.

    The next day Canius invites his friends; he comes early himself and sees not a single boat.Cic. Off. 3.59

See also he, her, its, their, own.
